Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette:
The drowning happened on a Saturday afternoon in late August, at a crowded lake beach north of the city. Marcus had been twenty-two, still in his final year of pharmacy school, and his younger brother Koa had just turned nineteen. They had gone with friends to celebrate. Marcus remembered the heat, the way the air felt thick and wet, the sound of music from a portable speaker. He remembered Koa laughing, then wading out past the buoys, then the moment someone pointed and said, *is he okay?* The next hour was a blur he could never reassemble into a clear story—he could only recall fragments: a lifeguard shouting, the strange stillness of the water, the way his own legs would not move. Koa did not survive. The official report said a sudden cramp, possibly alcohol-related; there had been a cooler of beer on the beach. Marcus had not touched alcohol since.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself unable to hold the event in his mind as a coherent narrative. When he tried to remember, he would either feel nothing at all—a flat, hollow numbness, as if the memory belonged to someone else—or he would be struck by a wave of guilt so sharp it doubled him over. He should have been watching. He should have said something when Koa went out past the buoys. He should have been a better older brother. These thoughts came without warning, triggered by things that seemed unrelated: the smell of beer on a customer’s breath at the pharmacy, the sight of a funeral procession from the store window, the sound of a group of people laughing too loudly. Each time, the memory would surge back—fragmented, unbearable—and Marcus would feel his body tense as if he were still standing on that beach, helpless.

He worked at a chain pharmacy in a strip mall, and the job had become a daily minefield. The smell of alcohol was the worst: a patient would lean across the counter, and the faint sour note on their breath would send Marcus’s stomach into freefall. His body would react before his mind caught up—his heart pounding, his palms slick, his shoulders locked—and he would realize, seconds later, that he was not in danger at all. Nothing was wrong. But his body stayed on alert, tense and ready, as if the threat were still there. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by that afternoon, that the person he used to be—someone who laughed easily, who felt hopeful about the future—was gone forever. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. He went to work, he came home, he stared at the wall. He had stopped seeing his friends because their sympathy made him feel worse, and because being around them meant the possibility of someone mentioning Koa, or of a drink being opened, or of a joke being made that felt too light for a world that had taken his brother.

The cycle tightened. The more Marcus believed his life was ruined, the more vigilant his body became, scanning every room for signs of danger. And the more his body stayed on alert, the more convinced he grew that he was broken, that he would never feel safe or happy again. The guilt, too, fed the vigilance: if he let his guard down, he reasoned, he might fail someone else the way he had failed Koa. The smells and the grief-soaked places he avoided—funeral homes, cemeteries, the liquor aisle at the grocery store—only grew more powerful in his absence, because he never gave himself the chance to learn they were not dangerous. He had stopped visiting his parents because their house still had Koa’s room, and because his mother cried every time she saw him. He told himself he was protecting them. He knew, somewhere underneath, that it was himself he was protecting.

What finally brought Marcus to therapy was a panic attack in the pharmacy break room, triggered by a coworker’s perfume that smelled, inexplicably, of lake water. He had called in sick the next day, and the day after that, and he had realized he could not keep living this way—half-present, waiting for the next trigger, carrying a guilt that would not fade. He was afraid that talking about Koa would make it worse. He was also afraid, for the first time in two years, that staying silent might be worse still.
